title: Persistent Red-Black Tree
prompt:
Implement a fully persistent red-black tree in Python. 'Fully persistent' means that insert and delete operations return new tree versions without mutating previous versions, and all previous versions remain accessible and valid.

Your implementation must include:

1. A Node class that is immutable (or treated as such — no mutation after creation).

2. An insert(root, key) function that returns a new root with the key inserted, maintaining all red-black invariants.

3. A delete(root, key) function that returns a new root with the key removed (or the same root if key not found), maintaining all red-black invariants.

4. A search(root, key) function returning True/False.

5. An in_order(root) function returning a sorted list of all keys.

6. A verify_rb_properties(root) function that checks:
   a. The root is black.
   b. Every red node has two black children.
   c. All paths from root to leaves (None nodes, considered black) have the same black-height.
   d. The tree is a valid BST (in-order keys are strictly increasing).
   Return True if all properties hold, False otherwise.

Red-black tree invariants:
- Every node is red or black.
- The root is black.
- All leaves (None/NIL) are black.
- A red node's children are both black.
- Every path from a node to its descendant leaves has the same number of black nodes.

Path copying: since nodes are immutable, insertion/deletion must copy all nodes on the path from root to the modified position. Rotations must also copy affected nodes. Uncle-checking during rebalancing requires careful handling because the uncle may be in a part of the tree that was NOT copied.

Test your implementation:

Test 1 — Persistence:
  t0 = None (empty tree)
  t1 = insert(t0, 10)
  t2 = insert(t1, 20)
  t3 = insert(t2, 30)
  t4 = insert(t3, 15)
  # All four versions must be independently valid:
  assert in_order(t1) == [10]
  assert in_order(t2) == [10, 20]
  assert in_order(t3) == [10, 20, 30]
  assert in_order(t4) == [10, 15, 20, 30]
  assert verify_rb_properties(t1)
  assert verify_rb_properties(t2)
  assert verify_rb_properties(t3)
  assert verify_rb_properties(t4)

Test 2 — Delete:
  t5 = delete(t4, 20)
  assert in_order(t5) == [10, 15, 30]
  assert in_order(t4) == [10, 15, 20, 30]  # t4 unchanged
  assert verify_rb_properties(t5)

Test 3 — Stress:
  import random
  random.seed(42)
  keys = random.sample(range(1000), 100)
  tree = None
  versions = [tree]
  for k in keys:
      tree = insert(tree, k)
      versions.append(tree)
  # All 101 versions must be valid
  for v in versions:
      assert verify_rb_properties(v)
  # Delete half the keys
  for k in keys[:50]:
      tree = delete(tree, k)
  assert verify_rb_properties(tree)
  assert len(in_order(tree)) == 50
  # Original versions still intact
  assert len(in_order(versions[100])) == 100

Provide the complete Python code and show all tests passing.
verification_method: Run the code. All three test blocks must pass without assertion errors. Verify that verify_rb_properties correctly checks all four red-black invariants. The stress test (100 insertions + 50 deletions, all versions valid) is the key correctness check. Mutation detection: after the stress test, verify that versions[50] still has exactly 50 elements (path copying must not have mutated it).
why_frontier_hard: Path copying during rotations is the primary failure mode. In a mutable red-black tree, rotations modify nodes in place. In the persistent version, every rotation must copy the rotated nodes AND their parents up to the root. Uncle-checking during insert fixup requires accessing the uncle node, which may be in a shared (non-copied) part of the tree — the model must navigate between the new path-copied spine and the old shared nodes. Delete is especially treacherous: the double-black fixup cases require sibling access, and the sibling may or may not have been copied. Most models produce code that passes simple inserts but fails on delete or corrupts old versions.
ground_truth_notes: A correct persistent red-black tree uses O(log n) new nodes per operation (path copying). All five RB invariants must hold for every version. The delete operation requires handling: (1) deleting a red leaf (simple), (2) deleting a black node with one red child (recolour), (3) deleting a black leaf (double-black fixup with 4 cases). Each case must path-copy correctly.
